title: Title
notes: Open by separating the topological knot from the extra contact-geometric datum. A smooth knot in a 3-manifold can be moved in many ways, but once a contact plane field is present, the angle between the tangent direction and the planes becomes structure. This lecture follows that angle through diagrams, push-offs, linking numbers, and finally the classical invariants.

title: Contact Incidence
notes: The contact form turns a geometric picture into an equation along the knot. Legendrian knots solve the equation alpha on the velocity equals zero, so the tangent line is always contained in the contact plane. Transverse knots deliberately avoid that equation and keep a fixed sign. Emphasize that changing alpha by a positive function does not change these incidence notions.

title: Local Push-Offs
notes: Push-offs are the bridge from local contact geometry to topological invariants. The same embedded circle can be copied in many normal directions, but the contact planes provide a preferred family. Once the copy sits on the boundary torus, its homology class and linking number record how much the chosen framing twists around the original knot.

title: Convention Warning
notes: Pause here because many sign errors later are convention errors rather than mathematical misunderstandings. The source chapter uses alpha equal to dz plus x dy, so the front is the yz-plane and the missing coordinate is x. The notebook artifact is still useful, but it was computed in the dz minus y dx convention, so every formula involving slope must be translated before comparison.

title: Front Projection
notes: The contact equation makes fronts powerful. In ordinary projection one expects to lose information, but a Legendrian front recovers the missing coordinate by differentiating the visible curve. At a cusp, the projected curve has a singularity while the lifted Legendrian remains smooth. Mention the local JSON check because it ties the diagram to a sampled residual in the actual contact equation.

title: Lagrangian Projection
notes: The Lagrangian projection loses z instead of x, so the contact equation becomes a reconstruction formula. Integrating minus x dy along the projected path tells us the change in z. For a closed Legendrian knot, the total signed area has to vanish. This gives a different visual language from the front: crossings and area lobes become especially visible.

title: Transverse Fronts
notes: Contrast this with the Legendrian front. For Legendrian knots, the front itself determines the missing coordinate almost everywhere. For transverse knots, the key datum is the strict sign of alpha on the velocity, so one checks a proposed lift rather than solving equality. This is why transverse diagrams carry inequality rules and why a zero-contact event is the real forbidden feature.

title: Approximation Theorem
notes: The approximation theorem should feel plausible from the front picture. The contact equation asks us to prescribe a slope-dependent coordinate, and small front zig-zags give enough freedom to do that while staying close to the original curve in space. Stress the topology versus geometry distinction: the image moves little, but the tangent behavior changes dramatically.

title: Parametric Approximation
notes: Use this slide to make the approximation theorem operational. A single curve is handled by inserting local zig-zags, while a family requires choices that vary coherently. A shared subdivision and a standard two-cusp block provide that coherence. This is also a good moment to foreshadow stabilization: adding zig-zags changes classical invariants.

title: Linking Interlude
notes: Before defining Thurston-Bennequin, remind students how a push-off is measured topologically. The boundary of a tubular neighborhood has a longitude direction and a meridian direction. A preferred push-off may follow the longitude but also wind meridionally; that meridional coefficient is what linking detects. This is the topological accounting system for framings.

title: Seifert Surface Linking
notes: This slide grounds linking in a surface calculation. Choose a Seifert surface for the original knot, push the companion knot off so it intersects the surface transversely, and count signed intersections. The definition is independent of the chosen surface in the usual homological setting, which is why it can serve as a stable invariant for the contact push-off.

title: Diagrammatic Linking
notes: Students often know linking as a diagrammatic count, so connect that count back to the Seifert surface definition. The factor of one half appears when summing all crossings between two oriented components. For close push-offs, there is a convenient equivalent count using the undercrossings of the pushed copy. This is the computational form we need for Thurston-Bennequin.

title: Thurston-Bennequin
notes: Define Thurston-Bennequin as a linking number, not as a front formula first. The front formula is a computation method; the invariant itself compares the contact framing against a chosen Seifert surface framing. For null-homologous knots the surface is part of the notation because rotation and self-linking also depend on that homological choice.

title: Front Invariants
notes: Now the diagrammatic formulas make sense: writhe is a linking-style crossing count, while cusps correct the contact push-off in the front projection. The rotation number is different in nature; it measures the winding of the tangent direction in the contact planes, and the front converts that winding into signed cusp counts. Use the JSON table as a quick arithmetic audit.

title: Restrictions
notes: Use the lattice to show that the formulas are constrained by geometry, not arbitrary combinatorics. The Bennequin inequality bounds how positive the contact framing and rotation can be relative to a Seifert surface. The parity condition cuts the lattice further. For the unknot, this produces the familiar staircase beginning at the maximal standard unknot.

title: Transverse Invariants
notes: End the invariant story by relating transverse knots back to Legendrian knots. A Legendrian knot has two natural transverse push-offs, and their self-linking numbers combine the Thurston-Bennequin and rotation numbers with opposite signs. This formula explains why Legendrian data is finer: it contains two transverse self-linking values rather than just one.

title: Recap Exercise
notes: Close with a computation students can do aloud. They should first identify the diagrammatic data, then apply the formulas rather than guessing from the picture. The final recap connects the three languages of the chapter: incidence equations, projections, and linking numbers. That connection is what makes these invariants useful in later surgery constructions.
